Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For police violence, water/flooding and soil/outdoor smells are hard to reconcile as primary trauma-linked triggers when the rest of the profile contains no content suggesting a water, outdoor, or environmental trauma context. Bus riding could fit policing/public surveillance, but these other triggers point toward a different trauma setting.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
issues.explanation: The appraisal of lost connection to community/culture is possible after police violence, but in this profile it is not supported by the selected triggers or memories, which center on acute sensory reliving and bodily threat rather than social exclusion, community rupture, or cultural shame. It feels disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, emotionless recall can coexist with reliving, but combining complete numb detachment with full multisensory reliving and bodily reenactment as parallel core memory experiences is somewhat tensioned. More importantly, the reliving items imply a very specific embodied trauma scene, yet the trigger set does not reflect cues plausibly tied to that scene.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: Mirror checking is difficult to explain from the rest of the profile. The threat items concern rapid bodily danger detection, reading faces, and sleep vigilance; the memories concern reliving; and the appraisals concern distrust/contamination/community loss. Mirror checking suggests appearance/body checking or checking for signs on oneself, but no associated appraisal or memory content supports it. It does not cohere well with the police violence formulation here.

vignette:
Priya is a 25-year-old South Asian American woman who works as a counselor at a community mental health center in a mid-sized city. She presents for treatment approximately eight months after an incident in which she was forcibly detained by police officers while waiting at a bus stop near her workplace. According to her account, she had been sitting on a bench in the early evening when two officers approached her in response to a call about a disturbance in the area. Without explanation, she was pulled to her feet, pressed against a chain-link fence, and held face-down on the ground for several minutes while officers radioed for confirmation of her identity. She described the smell of the damp earth and grass beneath her face, the weight of a knee against her back, and the sound of passing traffic as bystanders slowed but did not stop. By the time she was released with no charges, her blouse was torn and her hands were shaking so badly she could not hold her phone.

In the weeks that followed, Priya found herself unable to board the bus she had taken to work every day for three years. She began driving a colleague's car on borrowed permission, and when that arrangement ended, she simply stopped going into the office, transitioning to telehealth sessions without formally explaining why. Her clients noticed the change in setting; her supervisor asked questions she deflected with professional ease. She had come to believe that something essential about her judgment had been compromised - that if she had missed the danger then, she could miss it again anywhere, at any time. Riding the bus now meant sitting enclosed with strangers whose faces she could not monitor, and so she did not ride it.

The smell of soil or cut grass - common enough in the park beside her apartment building - began to reach her before she could prepare herself. On mornings when the grounds crew had been working, she would find herself frozen in the doorway, her heart already accelerating, her body having registered something her mind had not yet named. She had started checking the mirrors in her apartment compulsively before leaving, and when walking, she kept her eyes moving across the faces of people ahead of her, reading microexpressions for signs of aggression or contempt. At night she lay awake with her back against the wall, certain that sleep would cost her something she could not afford to lose.

When the memories surfaced fully, they did not feel like memories. The pressure returned across her shoulder blades, her cheek felt the cold ground, and the damp smell rose around her as completely as if she were still there. At other times the same event came to her in a way that felt entirely evacuated - she could narrate it calmly, in sequence, as though recounting something that had happened to a patient in a case file, and she found that version almost more disturbing than the other. She had begun covering her face with her hands in moments she could not predict, in the middle of sessions, at the grocery store, in her car.

She stopped seeing the friends she had known before the incident - the women from her temple, the cousins who texted her about family gatherings she no longer attended. She had come to feel that she was no longer legible to them, that whatever she had been within that community was now inaccessible to her, and she could not explain why without saying things she was not ready to say. She had also come to feel, in a way she found shameful given her training, that she was somehow marked by what had happened - that it had left something on her that others might sense.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a session in which a client described being stopped by police, and she recognized, with clinical clarity, that she had not been present for a single word of it. She had been on the ground outside a bus stop, eight months ago, unable to move. She came to intake hoping, above all, to be able to do her job. What she feared most was that the person who had been good at it was no longer there to recover.
